title: Easy does it for young Irishman at Piazza di Siena
content:
Much has been made of equestrian sport’s unique capacity to field competitors well into their seventies, who profess that the key to longevity – and success – is a lifetime of learning the intricacies both of the sport and the horses essential to it.

But for 21-year-old Irishman Tom Wachman, age is nothing but a number: though many of his rivals today had three decades of experience on him, he piloted Do It Easy to a decisive victory in the Loro Piana Trophy, Saturday’s feature class at the CSIO Roma Piazza di Siena, a CSIO5* show jumping team competition.

61 horses and riders presented for the first round of the class, eyeing up a share of the €105,500 (£91,390; $122,421) prize pot and, perhaps more covetably, a final chance at qualifying for Sunday’s Rolex Grand Prix, one of showjumping’s most prestigious classes. 13 of those 61 would execute the clear rounds required to move into the jump-off, held over a shortened and reimagined version of the first round’s course, and replete with ferociously tough turns that dared riders to take major risks in pursuit of the fastest time of the afternoon.

The tone was set early on in this jump-off session by Brazil’s Yuri Mansur, the reigning titleholder in the Piazza di Siena’s Grand Prix. Riding Mister Jup in the pathfinder position, he set a blistering pace to stop the clock at 35.87 – but midway through his round, he sent a pole tumbling out of its cups. That mistake forfeited his bid on victory today.

All eyes then turned to early contender Richard Vogel of Germany, who comes to Rome in extraordinary form, having taken a second Rolex Grand Slam leg when winning the Grand Prix of Aachen just last week. Though he wasn’t mounted on his winner United Touch S today, the twelve-year-old Cloudio is a worthy contender in his own right, and Vogel is showjumping’s Usain Bolt. Even so, they couldn’t quite catch Mansur’s time, logging a 36.58 but leaving all the fences up to take the lead at that stage.

On the one hand, Vogel’s early round meant that it looked as though the win might be signed, sealed, and delivered from the get-go – on the other, though, coming after the fastest man in the sport meant those brave enough could emulate his eye for an inside line and aim to ride it even tighter.
26-year-old Nina Mallevaey of France did just that, pairing slicing angles with a risky move: she opened My Clementine’s stride up into a gallop to the second fence, and never eased the mare back or checked her stride from then onward. Their time, an impressive 36.26, shaved three-tenths of a second from Vogel’s, temporarily catapulting the pair into the lead.

But it was Wachman who topped the podium after delivering a performance that broke the finish beams on 35.95 – still nearly a tenth of a second slower than pathfinder Mansur, but clear and, as such, victorious. His efficient round aboard Do It Easy never looked rushed, but instead, relied on tactical line-finding and minimal adjustments to find fractional gains as he progressed around Uliano Vezzani’s course. In doing so, he did something no other rider managed: he put himself up on the clock in the first few jumps, allowing him to maintain the pace and balance on the back end of the track rather than chasing down the seconds over the final fences.

That also allowed him to make up for his horse’s clean, athletic jumping efforts, which saw him sail high over the tops of the jumps – a technique that’s a boon when the goal is a clear round, but can lead to accumulative mid-air delays.

But this isn’t Wachman’s first rodeo: he and Do It Easy also won the CSI5* Grand Prix at the London International Horse Show in December, making the then-20-year-old the youngest-ever winner of that prestigious class.

“It was a good course – it was quite difficult, quite delicate,” said Wachman. “It took plenty of jumping, so I was delighted with my horse today. It’s an amazing show, very rich in history and tradition. I’m so delighted to be here.”

Fellow Irishman Cian O’Connor made it into the jump-off but finished fourth after logging a 36.70 finishing time, but losing out on the win here will have been sweetened by the fact that Wachman is his student, and has trained under him since he was a child on ponies. Together, the pair ride under the Coolmore Stables banner, a subsidiary of the Coolmore racing empire helmed by Wachman’s grandfather, Irish business magnate John Magnier. The luck of the Irish, indeed: this is the country’s third consecutive win in this class.

“Tom is an extremely hard worker and wants to win above all else,” said O’Connor. He shows great grit and determination while always sympathetic and kind with his horses.

“In this sport we are all aware of the ups and downs but Tom is very humble and knows both sides of the coin. It’s a pleasure to work with him every day and to have been a little part of his journey from ponies to the highest levels of our sport.

“The LA Olympics are certainly a goal but a lot of work to be done between now and then and we will just keep our heads downs and enjoy the journey together.”

Now, the finale of the CSIO Roma Piazza di Siena looms. Tomorrow’s Rolex Grand Prix of Rome will feature 45 combinations, who have qualified throughout the week of competition. Wachman will be there; so, too, will Vogel, with a point to prove after his rare jump-off loss today.

Wachman’s compatriot Denis Lynch will pathfind with the exceptional Vistogrand, a veritable explosion of energy with hooves who has had the handbrake on so far this week in preparation for the main event; Yuri Mansur, early in the draw, will aim to retain his title and hoist the Brazilian flag above the umbrella pines yet again. It will be one of our most compelling glimpses of form ahead of the FEI World Championships yet this year – and a chance for one of the world’s best riders, or one of a selection of underdogs, to make Rome his empire.

– Tilly Berendt
